reference.source: Harrison's Principles of Internal Medicine / WHO / India NTEP
clinicalPearls: A sexually transmitted cause of genital ulceration produced by the Gram-negative coccobacillus Haemophilus ducreyi, now uncommon but still important in the differential of genital ulcer disease
The ulcer is typically painful, non-indurated (soft) with a ragged undermined edge and a purulent base, contrasting with the painless firm ulcer of primary syphilis
Tender, often unilateral inguinal lymphadenopathy that may become fluctuant and suppurate into a bubo is characteristic
The combination of one or more painful genital ulcers with suppurative inguinal nodes strongly suggests chancroid
Culture requires special enriched media and is insensitive, so diagnosis is often clinical after excluding syphilis and herpes; molecular testing is most reliable where available
Because genital ulcer disease facilitates HIV transmission, testing for HIV and syphilis is essential, with follow-up serology as needed
Treatment uses recommended antibiotics such as a macrolide, ceftriaxone or a fluoroquinolone, and fluctuant buboes may require needle aspiration or incision
reference.pathophysiology: Haemophilus ducreyi enters through breaks in genital epithelium during sexual contact. It secretes a cytolethal distending toxin and other virulence factors that cause keratinocyte and epithelial cell damage, producing a necrotic, ulcerative lesion with a neutrophil-rich inflammatory infiltrate. The organism resists phagocytic killing and provokes a suppurative regional lymphadenitis. The disrupted mucocutaneous barrier and inflammatory milieu markedly enhance the risk of HIV acquisition and shedding, linking chancroid epidemiologically to HIV spread.
additionalDifferentials: Traumatic or fixed drug eruption ulcer
additionalInvestigations: Dark-field microscopy and syphilis serology to exclude primary syphilis
HSV PCR or culture from the ulcer to exclude herpes
Nucleic acid amplification or PCR for Haemophilus ducreyi where available
Gram stain and special culture media (low sensitivity) if molecular testing unavailable
HIV testing at presentation and on follow-up
redFlags: Rapidly enlarging or fluctuant bubo threatening rupture and needing drainage
Coexisting HIV infection, which impairs healing and alters treatment response
Failure of ulcers to heal after appropriate therapy, prompting reconsideration of the diagnosis
Extensive tissue destruction or secondary bacterial superinfection
reference.prognosis: With appropriate antibiotic therapy ulcers heal over one to two weeks and buboes resolve, though large nodes may need aspiration and healing is slower in people with HIV; untreated disease causes progressive ulceration and scarring.
pitfalls: Assuming a painful ulcer excludes syphilis or coinfection, when mixed infections occur
Incising a bubo when aspiration through healthy skin is preferred to avoid sinus formation
Relying on insensitive culture and missing the diagnosis
Neglecting partner notification and HIV screening
management: Treat with an effective antimicrobial such as azithromycin, ceftriaxone, ciprofloxacin or erythromycin to eradicate Haemophilus ducreyi
Aspirate or incise and drain fluctuant buboes to relieve symptoms and prevent spontaneous rupture
Provide analgesia and local wound care for the genital ulceration
Test for co-existing sexually transmitted infections, including HIV and syphilis, with follow-up serology, given that genital ulcer disease facilitates HIV transmission
Review shortly after starting treatment to confirm clinical improvement, expecting slower healing in people living with HIV
Trace, notify and treat recent sexual partners and advise abstinence until lesions have healed
